description: Understanding baseline...

Use a wider ResNet (WRN-16-4) with modern training techniques: CutMix augmentation, cosine annealing LR schedule, larger batch size with higher LR, and label smoothing. This is a fundamentally different direction from the baseline ResNet-20 - using a wider but shallower network with stronger regularization to push accuracy higher within the time budget.

Keep the ResNet architecture but increase depth to ResNet-56 (9 blocks), use the same normalization as baseline (std=1), add Cutout augmentation, use cosine annealing LR with warm restarts, increase weight decay slightly, and use Nesterov momentum. The key insight from memory is that the WRN approach failed due to too many changes at once (especially normalization std and CutMix), so this approach stays closer to the baseline while making targeted improvements: deeper model + Cutout + better LR schedule.

Try a different direction: use a PreAct ResNet-18 (larger model with pre-activation blocks), combine with aggressive augmentation (AutoAugment for CIFAR-10 + Cutout), use OneCycleLR schedule for fast convergence, larger batch size (256) with scaled LR, and moderate weight decay. This explores a different architecture family (PreAct ResNet) and a different LR schedule (OneCycleLR) compared to previous attempts which used standard ResNet with MultiStep or Cosine schedules.

Explore a different direction: use a PyramidNet-style architecture with ShakeDrop regularization, combined with aggressive data augmentation (AutoAugment + Cutout). Previous best was PreActResNet-18 with Cutout at 94.21%. This time, try a different approach: use EfficientNet-like ideas with a wider ResNet (WRN-28-10 or similar), but carefully tuned. Specifically, I'll use a WRN-16-8 with proper settings (keeping std=1 normalization that works), Cutout, cosine LR with no restarts (single cycle tuned to budget), and moderate regularization. The key difference from the failed WRN attempt is: no CutMix, no label smoothing, keep std=(1,1,1), use torch.compile, and a single cosine cycle.

Explore a different direction: use PreActResNet-18 (which achieved 94.21%) but enhance it with multiple advanced techniques: (1) CutMix + Cutout combined augmentation, (2) mixup data augmentation with probability-based switching between CutMix and mixup, (3) use SWA (Stochastic Weight Averaging) in the final phase of training for better generalization, (4) use a single OneCycleLR schedule carefully tuned to the time budget, and (5) use torch.compile for speed. The key new idea is SWA + mixed augmentation (CutMix/mixup) which hasn't been tried yet.

Explore a different direction: use a DenseNet-like architecture (DenseNet-BC with growth rate 12, depth 100) which is known to achieve excellent CIFAR-10 accuracy. Combined with test-time augmentation (TTA), Cutout, cosine annealing LR (single cycle tuned to budget), and torch.compile. DenseNet hasn't been tried yet and is a fundamentally different architecture from ResNet/WRN/PreActResNet. If DenseNet-100 is too slow, fall back to DenseNet-40. Also try using exponential moving average (EMA) of weights for better generalization.

Try a different approach: use PreActResNet-18 (best architecture so far at 94.21%) but with a carefully tuned single cosine cycle, combined with knowledge distillation from a self-ensemble (born-again network style), and test-time augmentation (TTA) to boost final accuracy. Key differences from previous PreActResNet-18 attempt: (1) TTA with horizontal flips at evaluation time, (2) carefully estimated total steps for single cosine cycle with no restarts, (3) gradient clipping for stability, (4) slightly larger batch size (256) with scaled LR for faster training.

Use PreActResNet-18 (best architecture so far) with a carefully calibrated single cosine cycle that matches the actual training budget (no restarts), combined with Cutout augmentation, EMA weights, and a larger batch size (512) with scaled LR using OneCycleLR for super-convergence. The key new idea is using OneCycleLR with a high max_lr and large batch size for faster, more effective training, plus proper total_steps estimation to avoid the restart issues seen in previous experiments.

Explore a new direction: use PreActResNet-18 (best architecture family, 94.51% best) but with a properly calibrated cosine schedule using CosineAnnealingLR with T_max set to match actual training steps, combined with progressive resizing (train on 24x24 crops initially then switch to 32x32 for final phase to get more steps early), AutoAugment CIFAR-10 policy + Cutout, and EMA with proper decay. The key new idea is using AutoAugment (not tried with PreActResNet-18 before) and a properly calibrated single cosine cycle to avoid the restart issues that plagued previous experiments.

Use PreActResNet-18 (best architecture family, achieved 94.51% previously) with a properly calibrated cosine annealing schedule that uses a conservative T_max to ensure the LR decays to near-zero exactly once without restarting. Key new ideas: (1) use TrivialAugmentWide (a simpler but effective augmentation not tried before) instead of AutoAugment/CutMix/Mixup, (2) use a warmup phase followed by cosine decay with T_max set very conservatively to avoid the restart problem, (3) use batch size 128 with LR 0.1 (proven stable combo), and (4) use torch.compile for speed. The main insight is to avoid complex augmentation schemes and focus on getting the LR schedule right.

Try a ResNeXt-29 (2x64d) architecture which hasn't been explored yet - it uses grouped convolutions for better feature diversity. Combine with the proven techniques: Cutout augmentation, cosine annealing with a very conservative T_max (to avoid the restart issue), Nesterov SGD, and torch.compile. The key new idea is ResNeXt's grouped convolution architecture which provides better accuracy-per-parameter tradeoff than standard ResNets or WRNs, plus using a carefully estimated single cosine cycle based on timing a few warmup steps.

The parent solution achieved 95.69% with PreActResNet-18. I'll make one key improvement: add test-time augmentation (TTA) with horizontal flips to boost the final evaluated accuracy. The model's predictions will be averaged over the original image and its horizontally flipped version. I'll also add a slight tweak to use a larger initial learning rate (0.2) since the model benefits from more aggressive early training, and extend the safety margin slightly to use more of the time budget.

The parent solution achieved 95.94% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + TTA. I'll add Mixup augmentation during training (with alpha=0.2) which provides additional regularization by interpolating between training examples and their labels. Mixup has been shown to improve generalization and works well with Cutout. I'll keep everything else from the parent solution (TTA, cosine schedule, Cutout, etc.) and just add this one technique.

Add CutMix augmentation alongside Mixup (randomly choosing between them each batch with 50/50 probability), which provides complementary regularization. CutMix cuts and pastes patches between training images rather than blending them, forcing the model to learn from partial views. This combination has been shown to outperform either technique alone. Keep all other settings from the parent solution (PreActResNet-18, Cutout, TTA, cosine schedule, etc.).

The parent solution achieved 96.03% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + TTA. The key improvement: increase the Mixup alpha from 0.2 to 0.1 (lighter mixup for less label noise) and add a channel-wise random erasing (RandomErasing) as additional augmentation on top of Cutout. Also, use a slightly higher learning rate (0.15) to enable faster convergence and better exploration early in training, and reduce Cutout length from 16 to 12 to find a better regularization balance with Mixup. The main atomic change is tuning the Mixup alpha down to 0.1 since the CutMix experiment (95.88%) showed too much augmentation hurts, so lighter Mixup may help.

The parent solution achieved 96.03% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + TTA + cosine schedule. The key improvement: add label smoothing (0.1) to the cross-entropy loss, which has been shown to improve generalization by preventing the model from becoming overconfident. Label smoothing is complementary to Mixup and Cutout - previous attempts with label smoothing used it alongside CutMix/complex setups that failed, but here we add it cleanly to the proven 96.03% recipe. I'll use a small smoothing value (0.1) to avoid over-regularizing.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + label smoothing (0.1) + TTA + cosine schedule. I'll try increasing the weight decay from 5e-4 to 1e-3, which provides stronger regularization and has been shown to improve generalization when combined with other regularization techniques like Mixup and label smoothing. This is a simple, atomic change that can help the model generalize better without adding complexity.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + label smoothing (0.1) + TTA + cosine schedule. I'll add Stochastic Depth (drop path) regularization to the PreActResNet-18, which randomly drops residual blocks during training. This is a proven regularization technique that complements Mixup and label smoothing by preventing co-adaptation of layers. I'll use a linear drop rate schedule from 0 to 0.1 (increasing with depth), which is standard for ResNets on CIFAR-10.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + label smoothing (0.1) + TTA + cosine schedule. I'll try adding AutoAugment (CIFAR-10 policy) to the data augmentation pipeline, which applies learned augmentation policies that have been shown to significantly boost CIFAR-10 accuracy. AutoAugment is complementary to Cutout and Mixup, providing diverse geometric and color augmentations. Previous attempts with AutoAugment failed due to other issues (wrong normalization std, bad LR schedule), but the current setup has proven stable, so adding AutoAugment should provide additional regularization benefit.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + label smoothing (0.1) + TTA + cosine schedule. I'll try using a slightly wider PreActResNet-18 (width_mult=1.25, increasing channels from [64,128,256,512] to [80,160,320,640]) to increase model capacity. This should provide better feature representations while still fitting within the time budget. The wider model has more parameters but the same depth, so training speed shouldn't decrease drastically. All other hyperparameters remain identical to the parent.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + label smoothing (0.1) + TTA + cosine schedule. I'll try increasing the batch size to 256 with a scaled learning rate (0.2) to get faster training and more epochs within the time budget, which should improve convergence. Larger batch sizes with properly scaled LR have been shown to train faster without sacrificing accuracy, and getting more epochs means the cosine schedule can decay more smoothly. I'll also add a slightly longer warmup to stabilize the larger batch training.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% with PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + label smoothing (0.1) + TTA + cosine schedule. I'll try adding an EMA (Exponential Moving Average) model with a high decay rate (0.999) which maintains a running average of model weights during training. EMA has been shown to improve generalization by smoothing out noisy weight updates, and it's complementary to the existing regularization techniques. The EMA model will be evaluated alongside the regular model at each epoch, and the best performing one will be returned.

The bug is in the EMA update for buffers: some BatchNorm buffers (like `num_batches_tracked`) are Long/integer type, and the floating-point EMA update fails on them. The fix is to skip non-floating-point buffers in the EMA buffer tracking. I'll also keep all the other improvements from the previous implementation intact.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% as its best result (with label smoothing 0.1, Mixup alpha=0.2, Cutout, TTA, cosine schedule). I'll try adding a second TTA augmentation: in addition to horizontal flip, I'll also average predictions from slightly shifted crops (center crop + 4 corner translations). However, to keep it simple and fast, I'll just add multi-crop TTA with 5 crops (center + 4 corners with small shifts) plus their horizontal flips, giving 10 total predictions averaged. This provides a more robust ensemble at test time. Additionally, I'll slightly increase the Mixup alpha to 0.3 for stronger regularization which may help generalization further.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% at its best (with label smoothing 0.1, Mixup alpha=0.2, Cutout, TTA, cosine schedule). Looking at the experiments, the best result was 96.21% with label smoothing=0.1. I'll try adding progressive training: start with a smaller crop size (28x28) for the first portion of training to get more iterations quickly, then switch to full 32x32 crops for the remaining training. This effectively acts as curriculum learning and allows the model to see more diverse examples early on. However, this adds complexity. Instead, I'll try a simpler approach: use a slightly longer warmup (1000 steps instead of 500) and reduce the safety margin from 90% to 85% to be more conservative with the cosine schedule, ensuring it fully decays. Also, I'll increase Mixup alpha slightly to 0.3 since 0.2 worked well and slightly more regularization with label smoothing could help. Actually, looking more carefully at the results: the 96.21% parent used label_smoothing=0.1, mixup_alpha=0.2, cutout=16. Let me try a different atomic change: use Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention blocks in PreActResNet-18, which add channel attention with minimal parameter/compute overhead and have been shown to improve accuracy on CIFAR-10.

The parent solution achieved 96.21% at its best. Looking at the experiments, the best configuration is PreActResNet-18 + Cutout + Mixup (alpha=0.2) + label smoothing (0.1) + TTA + cosine schedule. I'll try using TrivialAugmentWide as an additional augmentation in the pipeline, which is simpler and faster than AutoAugment (which previously hurt due to slowdown). TrivialAugmentWide applies a single random augmentation per image with random magnitude, adding diversity without significant computational overhead. The previous AutoAugment attempt reduced accuracy from 96.21% to 95.78%, likely due to processing overhead reducing effective training epochs. TrivialAugmentWide should be much lighter.

Additionally, I'll increase the warmup steps slightly and use a slightly lower initial LR (0.08) to improve training stability.

Specifically, I'll use T_0 set to roughly 1/3 of estimated total epochs with T_mult=2 (so cycles are: T_0, 2*T_0, 4*T_0... epochs), ensuring the final cycle ends near the budget. I'll also add a small amount of weight decay scheduling by using cosine warm restarts naturally. The key atomic change is switching from a single cosine decay to CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts with T_0 tuned to fit ~2-3 restarts in the budget.

Looking at the experimental history, the 95.69% baseline (no TTA/Mixup/label smoothing) completed 74 epochs with the cosine schedule fully decaying by epoch 67. The key improvement I'll try: use persistent_workers=True and pin_memory=True in the DataLoader to reduce data loading overhead, and more importantly, use a more accurate time estimation by timing a full epoch instead of just 5 steps (which can be noisy due to compilation overhead). I'll also try using num_workers=4 (if not already) for faster data loading. The main atomic change is to use torch.amp (automatic mixed precision) with bfloat16 (not float16 which was tried before) specifically to speed up training and fit more epochs within the budget, while maintaining numerical stability. BFloat16 has better dynamic range than float16 and doesn't need a GradScaler.

AdamW with proper weight decay and cosine schedule has been shown to converge faster and find better minima on CIFAR-10, especially with limited training epochs. I'll use a lower learning rate appropriate for Adam (0.001) with weight decay 0.05, keeping all other augmentation and TTA settings identical to the 96.21% parent.
